We have a friend in common, the retired sophomore. His concern: that I shall get it like that, in the right and righter of a green bush chomping on future considerations. In the ghostly dreams of others it appears I am all right, and even going on tomorrow there is much to be said on all these matters, “issues,” like “No rest for the weary.” (And yet—why not?) Feeling under orders is a way of showing up, but stepping on Earth—she’s not going to. Ten shades of pleasing himself brings us to tomorrow evening and will be back for more. I disagree with you completely but couldn’t be prouder and fonder of you. So drink up. Feel good for two. I do it in a lot of places. Subfusc El Dorado is only one that I know something about. Others are recently lost cities where we used to live—they keep the names we knew, sometimes. I do it in a lot of places. Brash brats offer laughing advice, as though anything I cared about could be difficult or complicated now. That’s the rub. Gusts of up to forty-five miles an hour will be dropping in later on tonight. No reason not to. So point at the luck we know about. Living is a meatloaf sandwich. I had a good time up there.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: His, And, Feeling

outputs.L1:
We have a friend in common: the retired sophomore. His concern is that I shall get it like that—in the right and righter of a green bush, chomping on future considerations. In the ghostly dreams of others, it appears that I am all right; and even as we move into tomorrow, there is much to be said about all these matters—these “issues”—such as, “No rest for the weary.” (And yet—why not?)

Feeling under orders is one way of showing up, but as for stepping on Earth—she’s not going to. Ten shades of pleasing himself bring us to tomorrow evening, and he will be back for more. I disagree with you completely, but I couldn’t be prouder or fonder of you. So drink up. Feel good for two.

I do it in many places. Subfusc El Dorado is only one I know something about. Others are recently lost cities where we used to live; sometimes, they retain the names we knew. I do it in many places.

Brash brats offer laughing advice, as though anything I cared about could not now be difficult or complicated. That’s the rub. Gusts of up to forty-five miles an hour will arrive later tonight. There is no reason not to. So point to the luck we know about. Living is a meatloaf sandwich. I had a good time up there.
outputs.L2:
We share an acquaintance: the former second-year student who has since retired. He worries I’ll receive it in precisely that fashion—amid the right, then the even more right, of a green shrub devouring thoughts of what lies ahead. According to other people’s spectral visions, I seem to be fine; and even as tomorrow continues, plenty remains to be said about every one of these concerns—these “issues”—including the notion that “the tired never get a break.” Still, why shouldn’t they?

Being under instruction is one means of making an appearance, though she has no intention of setting foot on Earth. Ten variations of self-gratification carry us into tomorrow night, after which there will be another return for more. I reject your view entirely, yet I could not feel more affection or pride toward you. Finish your drink, then. Enjoy yourself on behalf of both of us.

I practice this in many locations. Gloomy El Dorado is merely the one place about which I possess some knowledge. The others are cities lost only recently, places where we once made our homes; occasionally, they still retain the names familiar to us. Again, I do this in numerous places.

Impudent youngsters hand out advice while laughing, as if anything important to me could no longer be hard or complex. There lies the problem. Winds reaching forty-five miles per hour are expected to arrive later tonight. Nothing argues against it. Indicate, therefore, the good fortune we recognize. Existence is a sandwich filled with meatloaf. I enjoyed my time up there.
outputs.L3:
The speaker reflects on a mutual friend’s worries about what the future may bring and acknowledges the difficult, complicated issues that lie ahead. Although the speaker and the person being addressed disagree profoundly, that disagreement does not diminish the speaker’s deep affection, pride, or support. Instead, the speaker offers sincere encouragement as they both move into uncertain territory.

Throughout the reflection, memories of different places continue to surface—cities and landscapes that have been transformed or lost, even when their old, familiar names remain. These recollections create a strong sense of distance, change, and nostalgia. They also reinforce the idea that neither places nor relationships can be reduced to simple explanations.

For that reason, the speaker rejects easy advice and reassuring clichés. The matters closest to their heart remain difficult, tangled, and resistant to straightforward solutions. Yet, as uncertainty grows and turbulence approaches, the speaker chooses to recognize the good fortune already known. Whatever happens next, they can look back with gratitude and honestly say that they valued and enjoyed the experience.
outputs.L4:
I am not certain when uncertainty became a duty. Perhaps it happened on a Tuesday, between answering a message I had already forgotten receiving and buying bread I did not need. Someone once told me that a responsible person always knows what comes next. Since then, I have kept several calendars, all of which disagree. One says I am late for an appointment; another insists the appointment took place years ago; a third contains only a drawing of a small blue horse standing beneath the words, “Do not forget.”

I have forgotten what I was not supposed to forget.

This worries me, although not continuously. Worry, like a neighbor, comes and goes according to its own schedule. Sometimes it knocks politely. Sometimes it climbs through the kitchen window and begins rearranging the spoons. I ask what it wants, but it answers with questions: Have you called your mother? Did you pay the bill? Why did you say that thing in 2009? Are you becoming the person you promised never to become? I make tea for both of us. By the time the water boils, worry has usually left, taking one of the teaspoons with it.

Obligation is another matter. Obligation wears sensible shoes and carries a clipboard. It reminds me to be useful, punctual, grateful, informed, emotionally available, financially cautious, physically active, and asleep for eight uninterrupted hours. I tell it there are only twenty-four hours in a day. It tells me this sounds like an excuse. We compromise: I spend the morning doing what must be done, the afternoon thinking about what should have been done, and the evening forgiving myself for doing neither particularly well.

Memory does not help. Memory is less an archive than a room after a party. There are coats on the bed, glasses on the floor, music still playing somewhere, and nobody can remember who brought the enormous plant. I can recall the exact pattern of sunlight on a classroom wall when I was nine, yet I cannot remember why I entered the bedroom. I remember the smell of my grandfather’s jacket more clearly than his voice. I remember arguments in which I was unquestionably right, though everyone else who was present remembers them differently. Perhaps memory is loyal rather than accurate. Perhaps it loves us too much to tell the truth plainly.

People are like that too.

We promise to understand one another, but usually we only recognize familiar shapes in the fog. A friend says, “I’m fine,” and I hear the crack beneath the word. I say, “Don’t worry about me,” and secretly hope they will worry just enough. We offer advice when affection would be better, affection when silence would be kinder, and silence when someone desperately needs us to speak. Then, despite all this incompetence, we remain friends. We send ridiculous photographs. We remember birthdays late. We share food. We forgive each other for being difficult because difficulty is often just pain wearing an elaborate hat.

Love is even less organized. Love loses its keys, leaves wet towels on the floor, and asks what is wrong while chewing loudly. It knows the answer and does not know the answer. It can survive distance but be wounded by a misplaced tone of voice. It says, “Always,” while glancing nervously at the clock. Yet it also sits beside a hospital bed at four in the morning. It learns how much sugar you take. It saves the last piece for you and then pretends not to have wanted it.

There are days when I believe relationships are impossible. On those days, someone sends me a message consisting entirely of a badly drawn cat, and the argument collapses.

Meanwhile, everyday life continues its quiet campaign. The laundry reproduces in darkness. The refrigerator hums with private conviction. A single sock waits behind the radiator for conditions to improve. Outside, buses arrive early when I am late and late when I am early. The cashier asks whether I want the receipt, and for a moment the question feels philosophical. Do I want evidence that this happened? Do I need a record of milk, oranges, soap, and a chocolate bar purchased against my better judgment? I say no, then change my mind, then lose the receipt before reaching home.

At night I consider the future. It appears enormous and blank until I remember that the past once looked the same. Somehow it filled itself with kitchens, departures, jokes, illnesses, songs, mistakes, reconciliations, and cups of coffee gone cold. I survived days I had declared unsurvivable. I was changed by events I barely noticed at the time. Some doors closed. Others turned out not to be doors at all but paintings of doors, which explains the bruises.

I have often wanted clarity. I imagined it as a bright room where every object had a label and every feeling knew its proper shelf. But whenever clarity arrived, it stayed only briefly. Certainty hardened into doubt; plans became stories; answers produced smaller, noisier questions. Eventually I began to suspect that confusion was not an interruption of life but one of its natural conditions, like weather or gravity or finding crumbs in the bed.

This does not mean nothing matters. Quite the opposite. Because everything is temporary and imperfect, small acts become strangely important. Answering the call. Washing the cup. Saying, “I was wrong.” Bringing soup. Laughing at the wrong moment and then laughing harder because everyone else has started. Standing in the rain with someone who forgot the umbrella. Letting them complain. Letting them leave. Letting them return.

We are inconsistent creatures. We want freedom and instructions, solitude and witnesses, adventure and a reliable place to charge the phone. We resent routine until it disappears. We ask for honesty and then request a gentler version. We insist that life should make sense while repeatedly making choices based on hunger, weather, nostalgia, and whether the moon looks especially persuasive.

Still, morning comes. The kettle works. A bird shouts from a roof as if it has solved everything. Someone somewhere opens a curtain, misses a train, falls in love, burns breakfast, receives bad news, tells a joke, or decides to try again. None of these events cancels the others. Grief and delight sit at the same table, passing the salt.

So I no longer demand that the world explain itself before I participate. I do what I can, apologize when necessary, and keep a spare teaspoon for worry. I try to remember the important things, though I know I will forget some of them. I try to love people as they are, even when they are inconvenient, which is often. I fulfill my obligations imperfectly. I laugh whenever possible.

The blue horse remains on the calendar. I still do not know what it means.

I have decided to enjoy it anyway.
outputs.L5: His hands rested quietly at his sides, and for a moment, the world seemed to pause. He could not explain the feeling growing inside him—a mixture of hope, fear, and longing. It was his alone, yet somehow it connected him to everyone who had ever stood at the edge of change and wondered what would come next.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal, stream-of-consciousness prose poem that blends friendship, memory, weather reports, lost cities, clichés, and absurd statements like “Living is a meatloaf sandwich.”
counterfactuals.output:
At 7:15 the weather report predicts a seventy percent chance of forgetting, with scattered laughter moving in from the west. You call to say the sky has misplaced its blue coat. I tell you to check under the years, beside the box of birthday candles and obsolete maps.

We were friends before the river learned its lines, before Atlantis sank from embarrassment, before Pompeii became a postcard addressed to no one. Or perhaps we met Tuesday. Memory is a bad librarian: it shelves your face among thunderstorms, puts my childhood under *Minor Appliances*, and fines us both for returning the moon late.

Living is a meatloaf sandwich.

There, I said it, and immediately three umbrellas opened underground.

You used to say every cloud has a silver lining, but ours had receipts, loose buttons, and the tiny brass key to a city that never existed. We searched for it anyway. That is what friendship is: two people carrying a door through the rain, insisting there must be a wall somewhere.

Tonight, temperatures will fall into the unpronounceable. Expect fog in the kitchen, hail in the heartland, and isolated pockets of déjà vu near the coast. Motorists are advised to avoid the ruins of Carthage and take the long way home. Better late than never, says the clock, which has been dead for years and is therefore right about everything.

I remember your red scarf waving from the train, though there was no train and you never owned a scarf. Still, it waves. Still, I run beside it, my pockets full of weather, shouting the names of lost capitals while the houses turn into birds.

When the going gets tough, the tough become lighthouses.

When one door closes, another develops a mild fever.

It is what it is, except when it isn’t.

By morning, friendship will accumulate in drifts of six to eight inches. Schools will close. Statues will whisper. Somewhere beneath the avenue, an entire city will wake, yawn dust, and ask whether we remembered to bring the sun.

We did not.

So we bring each other.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an experimental paragraph in the style of a dreamlike collage, using non sequiturs, repeated phrases, strange metaphors, and an undercurrent of affection and disagreement.
counterfactuals.output: You said the moon was a locked hospital, and I said no, no, it is a spoon asleep in the garden, but still I held your coat while the elevators filled with seawater. Remember, remember: the blue dog barking inside the radio, the pears wearing little gloves, the afternoon folding itself into a paper knife. I disagree with your theory of rain, darling; I disagree with the way you name the birds after vanished countries, yet I save every name in a jar beneath the bed. Come back, come back, the furniture is learning to forgive us. Somewhere a train is pouring milk into the horizon, and somewhere your hand is an argument I cannot stop holding.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a piece of absurdist literary prose that sounds assembled from overheard conversations, forecasts, personal letters, and philosophical reflections. Include the line “I do it in a lot of places” twice.
counterfactuals.output:
At breakfast the radio announced a 60 percent chance of memory, increasing toward evening. Residents in low-lying neighborhoods were advised to move their childhoods to higher shelves.

“Did you bring the receipt?” a woman asked beside the window.

“For the rain?”

“For your brother.”

Outside, buses carried the names of extinct emotions. REGRET stopped at the corner, sighed hydraulically, and continued without passengers.

Dear Marina,

The post office says your address no longer exists, but I am writing anyway. Yesterday I found a small blue door behind the refrigerator. It opens onto a Tuesday in 1984. Someone there keeps boiling an egg. I have asked them to stop, but they say history requires protein.

The landlord came by wearing a crown of invoices. He pointed at the ceiling and asked whether I had been thinking after ten o’clock.

“I do it in a lot of places”

He wrote this down as evidence.

By noon, winds will turn northeasterly, carrying loose opinions across the municipal district. Visibility will be poor wherever certainty accumulates. Philosophers are reminded to secure outdoor furniture and avoid standing beneath unexamined assumptions.

On the train, a child held a dead telephone to his ear.

“Yes,” he said. “No. The king is made of soup.”

His mother apologized to everyone, though no one had complained. Across the aisle, two men discussed the price of teeth.

“You can get a full set in April.”

“April is imported.”

“Everything is imported now, even distance.”

It is possible that the soul is only the body’s way of requesting a window seat. This would explain the elbows. It would not explain cathedrals, but perhaps cathedrals are merely elbows raised against the sky.

Dear Marina,

I forgot to tell you that the dog has joined a committee. He leaves every morning with a briefcase and returns smelling of compromise. Last night he voted against the moon. The moon passed anyway.

Do you remember the hotel where the hallways grew longer after midnight? You said love was a form of poor navigation. I said nothing because the elevator had arrived full of snow.

A voice in the lobby asked, “Where do you usually lose yourself?”

“I do it in a lot of places”

The clerk handed me a key shaped like a question mark.

Tomorrow will be warmer, except in rooms where bad news has recently been opened. A dense fog of unfinished sentences will settle over the coast. Mariners should listen for bells, apologies, and the names they were nearly given.

At dusk, the city folded its streets and placed them beneath the courthouse. People stood where their homes had been and compared instructions.

“Mine says swallow whole.”

“Mine says keep away from direct sunlight.”

“Mine is just a photograph of a horse.”

The mayor appeared on a balcony to reassure us that disappearance was temporary, like employment or spring. Behind him, officials carried the horizon out through a service entrance.

Dear Marina,

If this reaches you, please return the enclosed silence. It belonged to my father, and I promised not to spend it all at once.

I have begun to suspect that existence is a rumor told by furniture. Chairs insist we are tired. Beds claim we are mortal. Mirrors repeat whatever they hear. Only the table remains discreet, bearing the weight of our evidence without comment.

Tonight there is a 90 percent chance of night.

Later, conditions will become indistinguishable from conditions.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a disjointed monologue narrated by someone reminiscing about friends and vanished places while jumping unpredictably between emotional confessions, nonsense imagery, practical advice, and impending bad weather.
counterfactuals.output:
I still dream about Marta’s apartment above the bakery, though both are gone now—the apartment folded into luxury scaffolding, the bakery replaced by a shop selling lamps that look ashamed of being lamps. Marta used to whistle through her teeth when she lied. I loved her, probably. Or I loved the blue cup she always gave me. Sometimes affection is just being assigned the same chipped object over and over.

There’s a storm coming.

You can tell by the way the pigeons negotiate with the gutters, and by the pressure behind the eyes. Bring in anything light enough to become a weapon: chairs, flowerpots, apologies. Tie down the lid of the bin. Charge your phone.

Daniel would have laughed at that. Daniel laughed whenever anyone prepared for anything. He kept a suitcase full of uncooked rice under his bed because a fortune-teller in Leeds told him to. When he disappeared—not vanished, exactly, just stopped answering—I inherited one of his coats and wore it until the elbows opened like mouths.

Do elbows know hunger?

The old swimming pool is a parking garage now. Level three smells faintly of chlorine in summer, though nobody believes me. We used to dive badly and surface shouting the names of extinct kings. The lifeguard had orange eyebrows. The vending machine dispensed, once, a live moth and two coins from a country that had not yet been invented.

If the power goes out, don’t open the refrigerator unless you must. Food stays cold longer in a closed room. So do grudges.

I should have called my brother.

No, listen—the clouds are turning the color of cutlery. The radio says hail, then flooding, then corrects itself and says “localized uncertainty,” which is how I would describe my twenties. Put towels along the sill. Keep shoes near the bed in case the glass breaks. Never shelter under a tree that knows your full name.

There was a cinema on Bell Street where June and I watched the same terrible film four times because the heating worked. She cried only during the advertisements. Years later she wrote to say she’d married a beekeeper and couldn’t remember my face. I stared at that sentence until the walls began filling with polite horses.

Maybe I wasn’t kind to her. Maybe memory is a landlord painting over damp.

The wind has started moving the bins. One just passed the window with great purpose, like a black plastic bishop. Somewhere, a gate is banging out a message I almost understand.

Marta, Daniel, June—if any of you are listening, I kept the blue cup. I lost the coat. I lied about the pool.

Fill the bathtub now, before the water turns brown. Find the candles, but use a flashlight if you can; candles make every disaster look more romantic than it is.

The first thunder is always a door closing in a house that no longer exists.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write one dense paragraph of uncanny, AI-like free association featuring a retired sophomore, a green bush, ghostly dreams, El Dorado, laughing brats, forty-five-mile-per-hour gusts, and a meatloaf sandwich.
counterfactuals.output: The retired sophomore stood beside a green bush that kept buffering in forty-five-mile-per-hour gusts, chewing a meatloaf sandwich shaped like a lost continent while ghostly dreams leaked from his varsity jacket and drifted toward El Dorado, where laughing brats in paper crowns counted backward from forever, their teeth clicking like tiny office machines, and every bite he swallowed became a hallway, every hallway a bell, every bell a gold-plated error message insisting that youth had been successfully uninstalled.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
